name: OPAL
aliases: Optimising Pelvic floor Exercises to Achieve Long-term benefits
question: Does adding clinic and home electromyographic biofeedback to supervised pelvic floor muscle training improve urinary incontinence outcomes in women with stress or mixed incontinence?

design.blinding: Participants, therapists and researchers unblinded; six-month pelvic floor assessors blinded

arms.label: Pelvic floor muscle training with clinic and home EMG biofeedback

design.population: Women aged at least 18 years newly presenting with stress or mixed urinary incontinence, able to contract their pelvic floor muscles, and without prolapse beyond stage II.
design.locator: BMJ full text, Methods: Study design and participants, Randomisation and masking; Results, Fig 1

verdictNote: The 24-month adjusted ICIQ-UI SF difference was −0.09 points (P=0.84).
takeaway: In OPAL, adding clinic and home electromyographic biofeedback to supervised pelvic floor muscle training did not improve 24-month urinary incontinence severity versus the same training without biofeedback in women with stress or mixed incontinence.

reports.label: Primary clinical report
reports.citation: Hagen S, Elders A, Stratton S, et al. "Effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training with and without electromyographic biofeedback for urinary incontinence in women: multicentre randomised controlled trial." *BMJ.* 2020;371:m3719. doi:10.1136/bmj.m3719
reports.followUpLocator: BMJ full text, Methods: Outcomes; Results, Table 3

results.measure: 24-month adjusted mean difference in ICIQ-UI SF points (EMG biofeedback minus PFMT alone; lower is better)
results.note: Superiority tested at two-sided 5% significance; 3 points used as the meaningful difference for sample-size planning.
results.locator: BMJ full text, Methods: Statistical analysis; Results, Table 3

results.measure: 24-month ICIQ-UI SF frequency or quantity response of never or none
results.locator: BMJ full text, Methods: Outcomes; Results, Table 4

results.measure: 24-month ICIQ-UI SF reduction of at least 3 points
results.locator: BMJ full text, Methods: Outcomes; Results, Table 4

results.measure: 24-month adjusted mean difference in self-efficacy points
results.note: This secondary measure favored biofeedback; clinical significance was uncertain.
results.locator: BMJ full text, Results: PFMT self-efficacy

delivery.label: Process evaluation
delivery.value: Therapist checklists and appointment recordings found that the biofeedback group received additional biofeedback components while basic PFMT components were delivered in both groups; optional components were seldom used. Therapist-recorded home programme adherence between appointments was 220/281 (78.3%) versus 241/297 (81.1%).
delivery.locator: Full text, Table 13, p 27; Process evaluation, pp 51–52, 61–62

delivery.note: Post hoc allowance for biofeedback introduction by appointment 2 gave 222/266 (83.5%) in the biofeedback arm.

delivery.note: Participant-reported exercise during the preceding month; once weekly or more often.
